display_title: Official Review of Submission1757 by Reviewer UHSv

summary.value: This paper introduces a technique (ED) to reduce hallucination in multi-modal large language models (MLLMs) by splitting an image into N sub-images followed by using an attention guided ensemble decoding approach which ensembles the logits for the next token to be predicted by the MLLM using the attention weights of the original full-sized image and the N sub-images with the text prior. The authors conduct a systematic study which shows the two main causes of object hallucination in MLLMs as the number of objects in an image and the image resolution. They also provide systematic quantitative metrics which show improvement on hallucination benchmarks compared to existing SoTA methods and regular decoding approaches. The authors present a latency analysis of their method compared to other decoding based methods and provide a alternative baseline of FastED which balances accuracy with speed. Overall the paper is well written and conducts systematic experimental analysis.

strengths.value:
1) The paper is very well written and it is easy to understand their method. 
2) The approach presented is easy to implement, is training-free and only requires inference time re-weighting of logits. 
2) The pilot study which talks about the main causes of object hallucination in MLLMs is instructive and useful to the community as a whole. 
3) It is easy to understand the motivation of their method from the conclusions of the study they present, which shows that masking irrelevant regions of an image helps reduce object hallucination, and their approach of ensembling logits from various sub-images should help with that
4) The results achieve SoTA performance on commonly used benchmarks to measure hallucination (POPE and CHAIR)

weaknesses.value:
1) While the idea of splitting the original image into N sub-images is well motivated from the pilot study, the approach to utilize the attention weights to re-weight the logits lacks theoretical/empirical justification. Even intuitively, it would make sense to use attention weights for prompts such as "is there a spoon in the image" to put a higher emphasis on the sub-image which contains a spoon. However, for generic prompts such as "describe the image", the attention weights across the sub-images should be more or less equal. In such cases I am not sure of the reason why it might be useful to weight the logits by the attention scores. 
2) Adding on to 1, the paper lacks experiments/ablations which justify the use of attention weights for the decoding process. Adding ablations which vary the temperature parameter might be useful to understand the impact of attention on results. For example, a useful result to conclude the validity of the attention weights could be setting very high values of temperature parameter leading to sampling from uniform distribution across the sub-images. 
3) The paper does not include experiments on tasks other than hallucination and image captioning. For example on the MME benchmark, out of the 16 tasks, the authors only include results on the existence, count, position, and color sub-categories. It would be good to look at the results on some of the other sub-tasks such as code reasoning, OCR, common-sense reasoning, text translation etc. (as done in the VCD paper) to ensure that this method of decoding does not regress the performance on such benchmarks. 
4) The authors show results for FastED only on CHAIR and LLava-Bench, it would be good to see results of FastED on POPE and MME benchmarks as well 
5) This is already mentioned in the limitations section, but the method only works for MLLM architectures which use a linear projector and does not work with resampler and Q-former based architectures (BLIP-2, Qwen-VL). This limits the generalizability of the technique across a wide-range of model architectures.

questions.value:
Please refer to the weaknesses section for questions. Additionally: 

1) Have you tried the recent Qwen-2 VL model with your technique? Given that it does not use a Q-former based technique, it would be interesting to see how this method works with a model architecture other than LLava
2) If possible, could you provide some additional examples of attention maps and final attention weights for the N sub-images for different sets of prompts and input images? It would be helpful to understand how exactly the attention weights vary.

Thank you for your positive evaluation of our pilot study and review of our method. Your detailed feedback has greatly contributed to deepening our research. We’ve prepared responses to your feedback and would appreciate it if you could take a look.

---

## **Weaknesses**

### **4.1 Impact of Prior Tokens on Attention-Guided Weights**

Our attention-guided weights are influenced not only by the prompt but also by the preceding output tokens. This means that all prior tokens are considered when calculating the attention-guided weights and generating the next token. The examples in Figure 6 demonstrate how attention weights are dynamically allocated to the most relevant regions just before the next token is generated. While the prompt remains fixed, the attention map continuously adapts based on the focus of the preceding tokens. This characteristic allows the model to produce more accurate and detailed descriptions in captioning tasks, as demonstrated by the improved performance on the CHAIR and LLaVA-bench captioning benchmarks.

----

### **4.2 Validation of Attention-Guided Weights**
To further validate the effectiveness of attention-guided weights, we evaluate the model's performance by assigning equal weights to all sub-images instead of using attention-guided weights. The results in Table R1 reveal a significant drop in performance when attention-guided weights are excluded. Additionally, we examine how varying the temperature parameter ($\tau$) impacts performance, observing a trend where lower temperatures generally improve outcomes. However, no substantial visual differences are detected in the outputs.

**Table R1. Results on the POPE COCO benchmark with and without attention-guided weights.**
| Setting       | Method                        | F1 Score | Accuracy |
|---------------|-------------------------------|----------|----------|
| **Random**    | ED (w/o attention-guided weight) | 80.68    | 83.6     |
|               | ED ($\tau$ = 1e-1)                           | 88.27    | 89.23    |
|               | ED ($\tau$ = 1e-2)                             | **88.84**    | **89.63**    |
| **Popular**   | ED (w/o attention-guided weight) | 80.02    | 82.9     |
|               | ED ($\tau$ = 1e-1)                             | 86.91    | 87.80   |
|               | ED ($\tau$ = 1e-2)                             | **87.34**    | **88.03**   |
| **Adversarial** | ED (w/o attention-guided weight) | 78.44    | 81.23    |
|               | ED ($\tau$ = 1e-1)                             | 84.53    | **85.17**    |
|               | ED ($\tau$ = 1e-2)                             | **84.59**    | 84.97    |

----

### **4.3 ED's Applicability to Other Tasks**
To further evaluate performance beyond hallucination and image captioning, we conduct experiments on other tasks in the MME benchmark. As described in Table R2, ED shows a noticeable improvement in tasks such as OCR, achieving a higher total score compared to the previous work, VCD. This result demonstrates that our approach is not only effective in addressing hallucination and image captioning but also transferable to other tasks.

**Table R2. Results on the MME benchmark comparing VCD and ED, evaluated with Accuracy+.**

----

### **4.4 Performance of FastED**
Equation R1. $f_{k,t} = \frac{\exp(s_{k,t}/\tau)}{\sum_{j=1}^N \exp(s_{j,t}/\tau)}$

As shown in Equation R1, decreasing the temperature value ($\tau$) enhances the focus on the sub-image with the highest attention score among the $n$ sub-images. This adjustment causes ED to produce results that closely align with those of FastED. Additionally, for tasks requiring concise answers, such as POPE or MME, the difference in inference latency between ED and FastED is negligible, making ED a suitable choice for such tasks. As a result, we plan to use results from ED in place of FastED for these scenarios.

----

### **4.5 Expanding Applicability to Diverse VLM Architectures**
Recent studies have highlighted the emergence of new VLMs that utilize linear projectors, offering opportunities to extend our method to a wider range of models [1-2]. Furthermore, VLMs employing resamplers (e.g., InstructBLIP, Qwen-VL) could adopt a similar approach by integrating an additional module to compute attention weights. While existing research on attention map formation is well-suited for prompts [3], there has been limited investigation into the use of dynamic attention maps at the token level within VLMs. We plan to address this gap as part of our future work.

summary.value: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) excel at tasks like image captioning but face challenges with object hallucination, where they describe objects that aren't actually present in images. While existing solutions like data augmentation have attempted to address this issue, they face scalability problems and often require additional modules. This paper introduces Ensemble Decoding (ED), which works by dividing input images into smaller parts and combining their logit distributions using attention map-based weighting. It also develops ED adaptive plausibility constraint for logit distribution calibration and a faster variant called FastED for time-sensitive applications. Through extensive testing on hallucination benchmarks, the proposed method demonstrates superior performance compared to existing approaches.

strengths.value:
1. It is interesting to explore the effect of the number of unnecessary objects in an image and the object resolution on the performance of LVLM.
2. The proposed method is simple and straightforward to implement, which enhances its reproducibility.
3. Experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed method can achieve better performance than state-of-the-art work.

weaknesses.value:
I have some concerns about this paper:

1. From Figure 3, it seems that feeding multiple sub-images into LVLM gives more correct answers than feeding the original image. I'm curious about the performance of ED without using the original image.
2. If LVLM produces the correct output for the original image, but produces the wrong output for the sub-image, does ED negatively affect the understanding of the model in this case? For example, can the split sub-image get a valid output when the target object is located at the centre of the image?
3. It is interesting that low-resolution objects may trigger the hallucination of large models. However, dividing the image into small sub-images does not improve the absolute resolution of the object but rather the percentage of the object in the image.
4. How is the metric of inference latency calculated? ED only slightly outperforms AGLA in terms of recall at the cost of more than twice the inference latency; FastED is close to AGLA in terms of efficiency but has lower recall. So what is the advantage of the method proposed in this paper over AGLA? The authors only show the performance of FastED on the CHAIR dataset, which makes its performance difficult to evaluate.
5. In this paper, there is a lack of analysis and ablation experiments on the impact of the constituent modules in ED (e.g. Attention-Guided Weight, and Adaptive Plausibility Constraint) on the performance of the method.
6.The exact number of sub-images into which the image is split (determined by the hyperparameter N) may have a strong impact on the efficiency and performance of the ED, and the impact of this factor is not analysed in this paper.
7. From Table 4, the improvement from aggregating the logits of sub-images does not seem to be significant.

comment.value:
Thank you for your insightful review, which helped refine and strengthen our work. We hope our detailed responses address your concerns.

---

## **Weaknesses**

### **3.1 Performance of ED without Original Image**

As explained in Equation 6, when $\beta = 1$ in our proposed ED Adaptive Plausibility Constraint (APC), only the outputs of the multiple sub-images are utilized, completely excluding the outputs of the original image. The performance of ED APC with $\beta = 1$ is shown in Figure 7. Under this setting, the average accuracy in POPE is the highest among all configurations, demonstrating that the outputs from multiple sub-images are sufficient to produce more accurate answers.

In our study, we set the $\beta$ to 0.5 to enhance generalization across various tasks, including scenarios where objects are incorrectly split or the overall structure of the image is critical, while balancing performance across multiple benchmarks. This effectively enables the utilization of outputs from both the sub-images and the original image.

---

### **3.2 Negative Effects of Sub-Image Outputs**

Such cases are possible, and we carefully consider this issue. To address it, as shown in Appendix B, we intentionally adjust the process to allow overlap between sub-images to prevent objects from being cut off (for more details on overlap between sub-images, please refer to **Questions 3.1**).

 As shown in Figure 7, the results illustrate that as the $\beta$ increases, signifying a greater reliance on sub-images compared to the original image, POPE performance improves. This suggests that sub-images are more likely to contribute beneficial information rather than introduce negative effects. Furthermore, we conduct additional experiments varying $\alpha$ when ED APC is not applied ($\beta=0$). As shown in Table R1, increasing $\alpha$ consistently led to significant performance improvements. This finding reinforces the conclusion that emphasizing sub-images has a positive effect on overall model performance.

**Table R1. Results on the POPE COCO benchmark with varying alpha values and without ED APC.**
| α | F1 Score | Accuracy | 
|--------------------|----------|----------| 
| 0 (Normal Decoding)| 79.67 | 81.40 | 
| 0.3 | 80.27 | 81.80 |
| 0.5 | 80.92 | 82.22 |
| 0.7 | **81.66** | **82.73** |

---

### **3.3 Maintaining Object Resolution through Image Splitting**

Our goal in splitting the image is to prioritize the resolution of specific objects that are important or relevant to the question, rather than focusing on the entire image. In our experiments, most images ranged in size from 400 to 600 pixels in width and height. Since the image encoder’s input size is fixed at $336 \times 336$, the conventional approach of resizing the entire image to fit this size significantly reduces the resolution of specific objects. To address this, we designed a splitting approach that preserves the resolution of target objects, allowing the model to process them with greater clarity.

---

### **3.4 Efficiency and Accuracy of ED and FastED**

Inference latency was measured as the average time to generate a single image caption under the same conditions. When examining the performance of ED and FastED more closely, both showed strong results in GPT-aided evaluation. Figure 5 presents the results of GPT's accuracy and detailedness measurements for captioning on LLaVA-Bench. ED and FastED outperformed AGLA, with ED showing particularly significant improvements in detailedness. 

Additionally, in tasks requiring short answers, such as POPE and MME, ED demonstrated superior performance compared to previous methods. This suggests that our approach offers a more comprehensive improvement over existing methods. Lastly, unlike AGLA, ED and FastED do not rely on external modules. This can offer advantages such as reduced latency, simplified design, and improved scalability.

### **3.5 Ablation Studies about Adaptive Plausibility Constraint and Attention-Guided Weights**

The results of ablation studies about Adaptive Plausibility Constraint (APC) is presented in Figure 7.  The figure reports the performance differences between the general APC proposed in prior research [1] and ED APC proposed in this study across varying $\beta$ values. On the x-axis of the figure, the $\beta$ values are shown, where $\beta=0$ represents the case where no constraint is applied during the decoding process. The results show that applying ED APC leads to better performance compared to using no constraint or the general APC, demonstrating the effectiveness of ED APC.

We also conducted an additional ablation study to evaluate the effectiveness of attention-guided weights. We assigned equal weights to all sub-images and compared the results with those obtained when attention-guided weights were used. As shown in Table R2, a significant drop in performance is observed when attention weights are not applied, emphasizing their crucial role in enhancing performance.

**Table R2. Results on the POPE COCO benchmark with and without attention-guided weights.**

| Setting        | Method                          | F1 Score | Accuracy |
|----------------|---------------------------------|----------|----------|
| **Random**     | ED (w/o attention-guided weight) | 80.68    | 83.6     |
|                | ED                               | **88.84**| **89.63**|
| **Popular**    | ED (w/o attention-guided weight) | 80.02    | 82.9     |
|                | ED                               | **87.34**| **88.03**|
| **Adversarial**| ED (w/o attention-guided weight) | 78.44    | 81.23    |
|                | ED                               | **84.59**| **84.97**|

---

### **3.6 The Number of Sub-Images**

As described in Appendix B, we selected the number of sub-images used in the main experiments to be 4, considering the size of most images (400–600 in width and height) and the vision encoder's input size ($336 \times 336$). Increasing the number of sub-images can help focus on smaller objects, but it also significantly increases computational costs. Additionally, it may result in each sub-image becoming too small, requiring upscaling when inputting the cropped images into the model, which could degrade performance. While this approach may be effective for datasets with larger image sizes, we leave this exploration for future work.

---

### **3.7 Improvement from Aggregating the Logits of Sub-Images**

In Table 4, we observe that, due to the influence of ED APC, the results remain robust regardless of the $\alpha$. To further investigate the impact of it, we conduct an additional experiment by removing APC and varying the value of $\alpha$. Table R1 indicates that performance improves significantly while increasing $\alpha$ without APC. Also, as $\alpha$ increases and the emphasis on sub-image outputs grows, performance improves. This highlights the importance of sub-image aggregation under these conditions.

**Table R1. Results on the POPE COCO benchmark with varying $\alpha$ values and without ED APC.**

| $\alpha$     | F1 Score | Accuracy |
|-----------------|----------|----------|
| 0 (Normal Decoding)| 79.67   | 81.40   |
| 0.3             | 80.27    | 81.80   |
| 0.5             | 80.92    | 82.22   |
| 0.7             | **81.66**| **82.73**|

---

## **Questions**

### **3.1 Overlap Between Sub-Images**

We deliberately allow overlap when creating the sub-images. Specifically, as outlined in Appendix B, for images with widths or heights larger than 672 pixels, we resized them to $448 \times 448$, ensuring overlap between the sub-images. This strategy was designed to mitigate issues arising from objects being split when located at the center of the sub-images.

To evaluate the effectiveness of overlap between sub-images, we compare our approach with a method where the image is simply divided into four parts without overlap. As shown in Table R4, allowing overlap prevents objects from being improperly split and significantly improves performance.

**Table R4. Results on the POPE COCO benchmark with and without overlap.**

|                | ED                         | **87.34**| **88.03**|
| **Adversarial**| ED (w/o overlap)          | 80.57    | 81.40    |

We sincerely appreciate you taking the time to review our response carefully and for asking such insightful follow-up questions. We have prepared responses to the questions below and truly hope they resolve any remaining uncertainties you may have.

---

### **3.8 Optimal Value of beta**

To further explore the optimal value of $\beta$, we conduct an additional experiment on image captioning using LLaVA-Bench, a task with a different focus from POPE. We vary the $\beta$ values while keeping other parameter settings unchanged. Alongside the default setting of $\beta$=0.5, we test additional values such as 0.1 and 0.01.
As shown in Table R5, higher $\beta$ values consistently leed to improved performance in terms of accuracy. A similar trend is observed for detailedness, though when beta is set to 0.01, the results are noticeably lower compared to 0.1 and 0.5, which produce almost identical outcomes. These findings suggest that while the optimal beta value may vary across benchmarks, increasing $\beta$ tends to enhance performance, helping generate more accurate and detailed captions for sub-images.

**Table R5. Results of GPT-aided evaluation on the captions from LLaVA-Bench with varying beta values.**

| Method | Accuracy | Detailedness |
|--------|----------|--------------|
| ED ($\beta$ = 0.01) | 6.14 | 5.92 |
| ED ($\beta$ = 0.1) | 6.72 | 6.50 |
| ED ($\beta$ = 0.5) | 6.93 | 6.46 |

---
### **3.9 High Resolution Achieved via ED**
In our pilot study, we intentionally reduced the resolution of individual objects within images to investigate the impact of resolution on object hallucination. Through this experiment, we observed that low object resolution exacerbates object hallucination, and this effect becomes more pronounced as the number of objects in the image increases. In most VLMs (as demonstrated in this experiment with LLaVA 1.5), the input image size for the vision encoder is fixed at 336 × 336, requiring the majority of images to be resized to smaller dimensions. This motivates us to explore methods for mitigating the resolution loss caused by this resizing process under such constraints.

Our proposed approach involves cropping the original image to create sub-images. By doing so, objects either relevant to the question or identified as significant by the model are preserved within the cropped sub-image. These cropped images already match the encoder's input size, eliminating the need for the typical resizing process that reduces the original image. Consequently, unlike using the original image as input, this approach ensures that the resolution of relevant objects is preserved, maintaining the original quality of the source image.


Thank you for pointing out this important aspect. We will ensure that this section is clarified and revised more thoroughly in the camera-ready version.

### **3.10 Performance of FastED**

To gain a deeper understanding of FastED, we conduct additional experiments on datasets requiring concise answers, such as POPE and the MME hallucination dataset. The results are presented in Tables R6 and R7.

These results indicate that, compared to ED, FastED tends to perform less effectively in tasks requiring longer answers, such as image captioning, while demonstrating comparable or slightly lower performance in tasks demanding shorter answers or prioritizing time efficiency. Based on these findings, it is evident that FastED is an effective model, offering both adequate performance and fast inference speed.

We appreciate the constructive feedback and the insightful questions, which provide valuable directions to further enhance the clarity and depth of our work.

---

## **Weaknesses**

As demonstrated in our pilot study, sub-images generally contain fewer objects and maintain a relatively higher resolution for each object compared to original images. This enables the model to better focus on relevant objects to text query, which is critical for mitigating object hallucinations and improving overall performance. Figure 6 further demonstrates that our method allocates higher attention to relevant regions, effectively mitigating hallucination compared to existing approaches. Additionally, various benchmarks on hallucination and description tasks validate the effectiveness of our approach. 

In Appendix B, we outline the rationale behind the degrees of cropping and resizing employed in the method. The crop size of $336 \times 336$ is chosen to match the input image size of the vision encoder (CLIP-ViT-L-336px [1]). Since most images in the experiments range from 400 to 600 in width and height, each image is split into four parts to balance the trade-off between capturing sufficient detail and avoiding excessive fragmentation. Further splitting could risk cutting objects or reducing the size of regions, which might negatively affect the results. Using a fixed crop size to divide an image allows for overlaps between sub-images, ensuring that objects near the boundaries are not improperly split. To evaluate the effectiveness of crop size and overlap, we compare our method with a baseline approach where images are divided into four equal quarters without overlap. As shown in Table R1, incorporating overlaps effectively prevents improper object splitting and significantly improves performance.

## **Questions**

### **2.1. Weighting in the Ensemble Process:**

As described in Equation 5 of the main text, the logits are weighted using their corresponding attention-guided weights, which are specifically designed to reflect the importance of each sub-image. Table R1 shows that the attention-guided weights consistently outperform uniform weights, achieving higher F1 Scores and Accuracy across all settings. These results clearly demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

---

### **2.2. Interpretation of the Relationship Between the Method and Model Uncertainty:**

Our method can be interpreted as an advanced approach to addressing model uncertainty by incorporating logical constraints rather than relying solely on simple averaging. The logits derived from sub-images reduce the influence of unnecessary objects in high-resolution regions, resulting in more refined and contextually relevant representations. Attention-guided weights prioritize key features, enhancing the reliability of ensemble outputs. This approach mitigates hallucination while aligning with uncertainty reduction principles, optimizing confidence and performance. 


---

### **2.3. Other Levels of Ensemble:**

We have not explored other ensemble methods in this study, but a potential approach could involve treating each sub-image independently, performing inference on each, and combining the resulting outputs using an off-the-shelf model. Further refinement and optimization of this agentic ensemble approach could serve as a promising direction for future research.

---

comment.value:
We appreciate your valuable feedback regarding our method and its relation to real-world deployment. Your thoughtful suggestions have inspired further reflection on our approach.

## **Weaknesses**
We acknowledge that our proposed ensemble decoding strategy introduces computational overhead, and we agree that it is not yet the optimal approach in terms of inference speed. Your suggestion of using a multi-image input strategy to process multiple images in a single feed-forward computation is indeed an interesting and innovative idea. This method could reduce computational costs and is worth further exploration.

However, implementing such an approach would require Vision-Language Models (VLMs) that are specifically trained to handle multiple images as inputs for generating text responses. Unfortunately, most existing VLMs, such as LLaVA 1.5 and BLIP-2, are designed and pre-trained to accept only a single image as input. Consequently, these models do not currently support multi-image input within a single forwarding step, limiting their applicability in this context.

For real-world deployment, we believe that a balanced approach is necessary, taking into account both sensitivity to hallucination issues and inference speed. Depending on the use case, different strategies such as ED, FastED, or Regular decoding might be more suitable.

---
## **Questions**
### **1.1. Dimension of $d$, $Q_t$, and $K_t$:**

In Section 3.1 (L161), $d \times d$ refers to the number of patches used by the image encoder of the 2D VLM. It depends on the VLM employed. For example, we used LLaVA 1.5 with a CLIP-ViT-L-336px [1] image encoder, which has $24 \times 24$ patches.

Regarding $Q_t$ and $K_t$, their dimensions follow the standard self-attention mechanism used in Transformer. Specifically, $Q_t$ is the query matrix at time $t$, with dimensions ($1 \times \frac{\text{hidden dimension}}{\text{number of heads}}$). $K_t$ represents the keys from time 1 to $t$, with dimensions ($\text{sequence length} \times \frac{\text{hidden dimension}}{\text{number of heads}}$). To improve clarity, we will revise $K_t$ to $K_{\leq t}$ in the manuscript.

---

### **1.2. Logit Ensemble and Adaptive Plausibility Constraint (APC):**

In our ED method, the logit ensemble is computed after forwarding $n$ split images individually through the same model. The final ensembled logits share the same vocabulary size as the LLM tokenizer.

The proposed ED APC emphasizes sub-image logits by filtering out logits below a threshold, ensuring such tokens are not amplified during the ensemble. It reflects our intuition that sub-images often contain richer details. As shown in Figure 7, ED APC consistently outperforms the original image-focused general APC used in prior work.

---

### **1.3. Handling Different Token Lengths:**

ED does not assume or constrain the length of generated tokens. Instead, logit distributions from sub-images are ensembled dynamically at each decoding step (as illustrated in Figure 3). If the end token is chosen in the ensembled logits, the decoding process terminates, similar to other LLMs/VLMs.

---

### **1.4. Hyperparameter Tuning:**

Hyperparameters $\alpha$ (in logit ensemble) and $\beta$ (in ED APC) determine the emphasis on sub-images, with larger values favoring sub-image contributions. As shown in Table 4, when ED APC is applied, ED demonstrates robust performance across varying $\alpha$ values. To further explore the impact of $\alpha$, we conduct additional experiments. Specifically, we perform ablation studies on $\alpha$ in scenarios where ED APC is not used  ($\beta=0$). The results, as summarized in Table R1, indicate that larger $\alpha$ values consistently lead to improved performance. This suggests that emphasizing sub-images has a positive effect on overall model performance.

**Table R1. Results on the POPE COCO benchmark with varying $\alpha$ values and without ED APC.**
| α | F1 Score | Accuracy | 
|--------------------|----------|----------| 
| 0 (Normal Decoding)| 79.67 | 81.40 | 
| 0.3 | 80.27 | 81.80 |
| 0.5 | 80.92 | 82.22 |
| 0.7 | **81.66** | **82.73** |



For $H$ and $K$, used in computing attention scores, we adopted default settings from prior work [2]. Exploring optimal values for these parameters is beyond the scope of this study but could be a potential avenue for future research.

---


[1] Radford, A., Kim, J. W., Hallacy, C., Ramesh, A., Goh, G., Agarwal, S., ... & Sutskever, I. (2021, July). Learning transferable visual models from natural language supervision. In *International Conference on Machine Learning* (pp. 8748-8763). PMLR.

[2] Lee, S., Park, S. H., Jo, Y., & Seo, M. (2023). Volcano: mitigating multimodal hallucination through self-feedback guided revision. *arXiv preprint arXiv:2311.07362.*

metareview.value:
The paper tackles the challenge of object hallucination in modern vision-language models. The authors propose an ensemble decoding strategy (ED) that feeds high resolution chunks of the input image to the model and decodes these chunks independently. These "ensemble" predictions are then combined together by using attention-based weights. The experiments in this work show that ED reduces hallucinations on POPE and CHAIR benchmarks.

Strengths
1. ED as a strategy is well motivated by the fact that image resolution is critical for correctly identifying details about an image
2. The FastED variant is also practically useful by trading off accuracy for speed
3. The paper is well presented and experiments are explained well
4. ED can be used for calibrating logit distributions 

Weaknesses
1. The paper trades off inference compute for accuracy. While this is useful, it does create practical issues.
2. I found the explanation for the attention based logit re-weighting hard to understand. It would be good to make this clearer.
3. The experiments are limited to a few datasets which reduces the impact of the approach. It would have been good to show that ED is more generally effective for object recognition.

Justification
This paper studies an important problem, is technically correct, and has convincing results. The paper also unanimously received positive scores.

additional_comments_on_reviewer_discussi.value: The reviewer concerns were addressed by the authors and all the reviewers remain positive about the work.
